newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges Congress to back MFN for China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Congress to back MFN for China.

text.p: President Bill Clinton asked U.S. business leaders on Thursday to support his decision to extend Most Favoured Nation trading status to China for another year.

In a speech to the Business Round Table, an association of business executives that has sided with Clinton in the past on trade issues, Clinton urged the leaders to speak out to members of Congress in support of his decision.

Some members of Congress are opposed because of concerns about Chinese human rights practices, allegations that Beijing is contributing to the spread of weapons of mass destruction and worry about the future of Hong Kong. A growing trade deficit with China is also contributing to their unease.
Last week Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, introduced a resolution to deny China MFN trade status.
House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, in a break with the administration, also opposes MFN status for China. A vote is expected later this month.

Clinton argued that China should continue to receive favourable tariff treatment on goods it exports to the United States in spite of what he called "great disagreements" with Beijing. He pointed out that presidents every year since 1980 had extended MFN to China.

"The question is, can we influence China best by treating them differently from all of our other trading partners for the first time in a very long time? Or can we influence them more by giving the possibility of genuine partnership?" he said.
He asked the business leaders to tell members of Congress in both parties that "this is not about whether we agree with China on every issue."
"It is about what is in the interests of the American people and what is most likely to give us the largest amount of influence and cooperation with China in the years ahead," he said.
He also said withdrawing MFN for China could jeopardise 170,000 export-related U.S. jobs.
